Adam Neely video essay Matt Schwartz blog post on writing a paper with Claude

Recently, I, like many people, have been occasioned to think more about what artificial intelligence—specifically large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, etc—is doing to affect the worlds of science and art. These two worlds are at first glance disjoint, but AI, across both fields, raises similar questions about what “progress” is, and what our role as humans is as producers and consumers.

Two essays that have made me want to write about this topic are (1) the video essay by Adam Neely on the rise of AI-generated music and how this is changing the landscape of music-making and (2) a recent blog post by Matt Schwartz on how he used AI to dramatically accelerate the process of research and paper-writing.

It doesn’t have to be a culture war: case by case basis is important

It is tempting to oversimplify the issue and take a single side: I think this is ultimately a position that lacks nuance. Both embracing AI as the savior of the world or declaring it as worthless miss the point: that AI is certainly helpful in some cases, but that our society’s apparent embrace of it in many spheres merits some consideration. I myself use AI on a somewhat regular basis, and it has saved me a great deal of time. But there have been moments of questioning what I’m doing, which, combined with the impetus from reading others’ opinions, makes me want to better organize my thoughts on this topic. My goal is to think critically about when, why and how we use AI.

Questions or answers?

The importance of friction

The process of being a scientist or an artist (and many other creative processes in life) tends to involve long periods of being stuck. For many people, there tends to be a large amount of friction in coming up with new ideas or even realizing a dormant existing idea. One of the things that AI does very well is reduce that friction. This capability is discussed at length in Adam Neely’s video. Matt Schwartz also remarks on the ease that AI lends to certain more prosaic tasks. This sounds like a very good thing, and I have personally experienced the fact that being able to use AI to get over the activation barrier, whether by writing a piece of code or doing a literature search quickly, can make a difference in whether or not I start something today or in a month.

AI makes us lonelier

I find tha interactions with other people are often the best part of both science and music. Sometimes these interactions can be driven by asking people questions. For example, if I don’t know about a topic that I want to learn about, but I know someone who does, I might ask them. I havve noticed that with AI chatbots at my fingertips, my first instinct is often nowadays to ask my question to the AI. Often this is productive, insofar as I get an answer to my question, often more quickly and more understandably than if I asked another person. In my experience, most of the time asking a scientific question of a person results in a longer discussio than just the answer to the question. People often don’t know answer to my question, which leads to a longer discussion or forces me to explain the quetsion differently. By contrast AI has such a breadth of knowledge that it can usually provide reasonable aswer. This fact means we can do more work, more efficiently, and crucially, in more solitude. This last point particularly strikes me as a point to consider. Is it a good thing to be working more on our own? AI is now certainly capable of functioning as a collaborator, but it is a strange kind of collaborator that does not have opinions of its own, never gets tired, and is willing to acquiesce to your every demand.
